COMPELLED SELF-PUBLICATION DEFAMATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's "compelled self-publication" doctrine in defamation law -- a body of case law addressing when the originator of a false, defamatory statement about why Jordan Lee's employment with Acme, Inc. ended can be held liable for defamation based on Jordan Lee's own later repetition of that statement to a prospective employer. It is a companion resource to, and distinct from, this project's Employer Reference Immunity information sheet (which addresses California Civil Code section 47(c) immunity for a reference communication the employer itself makes) and its Blacklisting a Former Employee information sheet (which addresses Labor Code sections 1050-1054). This document states California case law as background information. It does not determine whether any particular statement made about Jordan Lee's termination was, or was not, defamatory, whether any repetition of it was legally compelled, or what Acme, Inc. or Jordan Lee should say or do about any actual dispute.

THE GENERAL RULE AND THE FORESEEABILITY EXCEPTION
Under the general rule of California defamation law, a person cannot create their own defamation claim by repeating a statement to others; the publication element of the claim must be supplied by the defendant, not manufactured by the plaintiff's own disclosure. California case law recognizes a narrow, foreseeability-based exception to that general rule: where it was foreseeable that the defendant's act would result in the plaintiff's own publication of the statement to a third person, the plaintiff may still maintain a defamation action despite having done the actual repeating. This exception is often called the "compelled self-publication" or "self-compelled defamation" doctrine.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A plaintiff cannot manufacture a defamation cause of action by publishing the statements to third persons; the publication must be done by the defendant."
  — Live Oak Publishing Co. v. Cohagan, 234 Cal.App.3d 1277, 1284 (1991) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2135288/live-oak-publishing-co-v-cohagan/)
  "There is an exception to this rule. When it was foreseeable that a defendant’s act would result in publication to a third person, the plaintiff may maintain a libel action."
  — Live Oak Publishing Co. v. Cohagan, 234 Cal.App.3d 1277, 1284 (1991) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2135288/live-oak-publishing-co-v-cohagan/)
  Known gap: This clause states the general rule and the existence of the exception as established by published California appellate authority; it does not resolve, for any particular statement, whether the foreseeability exception would apply. The quotes below are drawn from a 1991 Court of Appeal decision that itself restates rules developed earlier (including in the case addressed in this document's next clause); it is not an independent, unrelated source confirming the rule from scratch. Research for this document was limited to a small number of published California appellate decisions actually read and quote-verified against their retrieved text (Live Oak Publishing Co. v. Cohagan, McKinney v. County of Santa Clara, and Tilkey v. Allstate Ins. Co.); it does not survey every California or out-of-state case discussing this doctrine.

THE DOCTRINE'S ORIGIN IN THE TERMINATION CONTEXT -- MCKINNEY V. COUNTY OF SANTA CLARA
California first recognized the compelled self-publication doctrine in the employment-termination context in a 1980 Court of Appeal decision. The plaintiff, a former probationary deputy sheriff, alleged his former employer gave him a false, defamatory reason for his dismissal, and that he was placed in a position of having to repeat that reason to police agencies at which he later sought employment. The court held that where the originator of a defamatory statement has reason to believe the person it defames will be under a strong compulsion to disclose the statement's contents to a third person after receiving it, the originator can be held liable for the foreseeable repetition -- because the causal link between the originator's conduct and the resulting reputational harm remains strong even though the plaintiff, rather than the originator, is the one who physically repeats the statement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The second context where this exception has been applied is where the originator of the defamatory statement has reason to believe that the person defamed will be under a strong compulsion to disclose the contents of the defamatory statement to a third person after he has read it or been informed of its contents."
  — McKinney v. County of Santa Clara, 110 Cal.App.3d 787, 796 (1980) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2147161/mckinney-v-county-of-santa-clara/)
  "The rationale for making the originator of a defamatory statement liable for its foreseeable republication is the strong causal link between the actions of the originator and the damage caused by the republication. This causal link is no less strong where the foreseeable republication is made by the person defamed operating under a strong compulsion to republish the defamatory statement and the circumstances which create the strong compulsion are known to the originator of the defamatory statement at the time he communicates it to the person defamed."
  — McKinney v. County of Santa Clara, 110 Cal.App.3d 787, 797-798 (1980) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2147161/mckinney-v-county-of-santa-clara/)
  Known gap: This clause describes a single published Court of Appeal decision from 1980; it is not a survey of how every California court has since applied or distinguished it, and it predates -- and has since been substantially engaged with by -- the more recent appellate decision addressed in this document's later clauses. The case was decided on a motion to dismiss, so the court's holding was that the plaintiff's allegations were sufficient to create a triable issue, not a final determination that the employer was in fact liable.

WHAT A PLAINTIFF MUST SHOW -- CURRENT ELEMENTS
A 2020 Court of Appeal decision -- addressed in full in this document's later clauses -- restated the doctrine's elements while applying it to affirm a jury verdict, and its restatement reflects California law as currently applied. To succeed on a compelled self-publication defamation theory, a plaintiff must show: (1) the defendant made a false, defamatory statement about the plaintiff; (2) the plaintiff was under a strong compulsion to disclose the statement's contents to a third person, arising from some necessity -- most commonly, a need to explain the reason for a job loss to a prospective employer who will otherwise learn of or ask about it; (3) the circumstances creating that compulsion were known to, or reasonably anticipated by, the defendant at the time the defendant communicated the statement to the plaintiff; and (4) the plaintiff in fact disclosed the statement to a third party. Because the plaintiff must actually have been compelled to repeat the statement in order to counter or explain it, a plaintiff cannot manufacture a claim by voluntarily repeating a statement with no such compulsion.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "For the exception to apply, the defamed party must operate under a strong compulsion to republish the defamatory statement, and the circumstances creating the compulsion must be known to the originator of the statement at the time he or she makes it to the defamed individual."
  — Tilkey v. Allstate Ins. Co. (citing Beroiz v. Wahl (2000) 84 Cal.App.4th 485, 497; Davis v. Consolidated Freightways (1994) 29 Cal.App.4th 354, 373; Live Oak Publishing Co. v. Cohagan, 234 Cal.App.3d at p. 1285; McKinney v. County of Santa Clara, 110 Cal.App.3d at p. 796), 56 Cal.App.5th 521 (2020) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4800305/tilkey-v-allstate-ins-co/)
  "This exception has been limited to a narrow class of cases, usually where a plaintiff is compelled to republish the statements in aid of disproving them."
  — Live Oak Publishing Co. v. Cohagan, 234 Cal.App.3d 1277, 1285 (1991) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2135288/live-oak-publishing-co-v-cohagan/)
  Known gap: This clause synthesizes the elements as restated in one 2020 published decision, which in turn cites several earlier California appellate decisions (Beroiz v. Wahl and Davis v. Consolidated Freightways among them) that were not independently retrieved or quote-verified for this document; only their restatement within the quoted source was verified. This clause does not state a damages standard (e.g., whether general or special damages must be pleaded) or a statute of limitations, neither of which was researched for this document.

CURRENT LAW -- TILKEY V. ALLSTATE INS. CO. APPLIED, DID NOT ABOLISH, THE DOCTRINE
In 2020, the California Court of Appeal for the Fourth Appellate District, in Tilkey v. Allstate Ins. Co., squarely addressed the compelled self-publication doctrine on appeal from a jury verdict -- the jury had found a former employer liable for defamation and awarded damages after the employer disclosed the stated reason for the employee's termination on a form the employer was required to file with a securities-industry regulator, a disclosure that was accessible to any firm considering hiring the employee. The employer argued on appeal that the doctrine should not support a defamation-per-se theory, that its statement was privileged and substantially true, and that punitive damages should not be available for a self-published statement. The Court of Appeal rejected the employer's arguments and affirmed that the doctrine remains valid California law, reasoning that the additional requirements of proving strong compulsion, necessity, and foreseeability already guard against a plaintiff manufacturing a claim, and that the doctrine does not, by itself, restrict an employer's underlying right to terminate at-will employment. Tilkey did not limit or narrow the doctrine; if anything, it extended it, holding for the first time in a published California decision that punitive damages can be available in a compelled self-publication defamation case -- while nonetheless ordering the punitive damages award in that case reduced to comply with the due-process limits that generally cap the ratio of punitive to compensatory damages. The defamation liability finding itself, and the underlying punitive-damages availability, were affirmed; only the dollar amount of the punitive award was reduced on remand.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Nothing about compelled self-published defamation limits an employer’s right or ability to terminate employment unfairly or capriciously."
  — Tilkey v. Allstate Ins. Co., 56 Cal.App.5th 521 (2020) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4800305/tilkey-v-allstate-ins-co/)
  "Allstate provided a written explanation for Tilkey’s termination of employment on the Form U5 to FINRA, which was available to every prospective employer of similarly-licensed employees."
  — Tilkey v. Allstate Ins. Co., 56 Cal.App.5th 521 (2020) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4800305/tilkey-v-allstate-ins-co/)
  "The slander here was self-published, but that does not change access to punitive damages."
  — Tilkey v. Allstate Ins. Co., 56 Cal.App.5th 521 (2020) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4800305/tilkey-v-allstate-ins-co/)
  "We affirm the portions of the judgment finding Allstate liable for defamation and punitive damages."
  — Tilkey v. Allstate Ins. Co., 56 Cal.App.5th 521 (2020) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4800305/tilkey-v-allstate-ins-co/)
  Known gap: This clause covers only the portions of Tilkey addressing compelled self-publication defamation and punitive damages; the same decision separately addressed the employer's use of an out-of-state domestic-violence diversion program under Labor Code section 432.7 (a wrongful-termination claim the court reversed on grounds unrelated to defamation) and an after-acquired-evidence defense, neither of which is addressed in this document. This clause also does not address a narrower, industry-specific privilege question the same opinion resolved -- whether the particular regulatory filing at issue was absolutely privileged under Civil Code section 47(b) as a communication in anticipation of an official proceeding (the court held it was not, on the facts of that filing) -- because that analysis turned on rules specific to securities-industry regulatory filings rather than on the compelled self-publication doctrine generally.

INTERACTION WITH THE CIVIL CODE SECTION 47(C) REFERENCE PRIVILEGE
The compelled self-publication doctrine does not displace the qualified common-interest privilege available under California Civil Code section 47(c) -- the same privilege addressed in this project's Employer Reference Immunity information sheet for communications an employer makes directly to a reference-checker. Published California case law confirms that this qualified privilege, which protects a communication about an employee's job performance made without malice to an interested party, is available to an employer as a defense even where the claim against the employer is framed as compelled self-publication rather than as a direct communication to a prospective employer -- because the compelled self-publication doctrine changes who physically repeats the statement, not whether a privilege defense to the underlying statement exists. As with any other application of section 47(c)'s privilege, it can be defeated by a showing of malice, and it does not protect a statement found not to be substantially true.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Additionally, the qualified privilege that attaches to communications about an employee’s job performance when made without malice or abuse to a third party likewise protects an employer against compelled self-published defamation."
  — Tilkey v. Allstate Ins. Co. (citing Cal. Civ. Code, § 47, subd. (c); Noel v. River Hills Wilsons, Inc. (2003) 113 Cal.App.4th 1363; Neal v. Gatlin (1973) 35 Cal.App.3d 871, 877), 56 Cal.App.5th 521 (2020) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4800305/tilkey-v-allstate-ins-co/)
  "This conditional privilege helps protect the free flow of reference information."
  — Tilkey v. Allstate Ins. Co. (citing Noel v. River Hills Wilsons, Inc. (2003) 113 Cal.App.4th 1363, 1373-1374), 56 Cal.App.5th 521 (2020) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4800305/tilkey-v-allstate-ins-co/)
  Known gap: This clause addresses only the qualified privilege under Civil Code section 47(c); it does not address the separate absolute privilege under Civil Code section 47(b) for communications made in or in anticipation of an official proceeding, which the same source decision analyzed in a securities-industry-specific context not generalized here. This clause states that the qualified privilege remains available as a defense; it does not predict whether that defense would succeed on any particular set of facts, which depends on whether malice or a lack of substantial truth is shown.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
This information sheet was prepared for reference regarding Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee on September 1, 2026, at Oakland, California. It states California case law as background information about the compelled self-publication defamation doctrine and is not legal advice about any particular statement, termination, or dispute.

Prepared by / on behalf of Acme, Inc.
Date: September 1, 2026
